review.summary: Model content review passed for the single objective, both simulation stations, and the harbor story. The supplied quotations support the attention distinction, and the formulas, illustrative values, targets, and reference settings are conceptually consistent. The transfer case changes the keys and requires a different value pair. Controls and visible targets support reasoning, and the fictional machinery is clearly separated from Transformer claims. This is not empirical learning validation or teacher certification.

episode.title: Special Delivery, Weighted Carefully
episode.subtitle: One bird, two attention experiments, and a parcel worth fetching.
episode.description: Piper explores a small harbor, comparing attention weights with the output they produce. Two numerical experiments earn passage across a bridge and access to a parcel platform. All numbers are illustrative—not learned language embeddings.
episode.briefing: Moss needs a parcel waiting across the harbor, and Piper has the wings—and the delivery responsibility. Help Piper complete Moss's attention experiment to open the bridge, then try Bea's changed case to raise the parcel platform. Carry one sample token between value-pair docks and use the query dial to compare visible weights and output. Collect the parcel and return it to Moss. The harbor machinery is a fictional reward for applying the model, not a demonstration of how Transformers operate machinery.
episode.ending: Piper returns the parcel to Moss, who holds it as though the harbor has finally kept a promise. “Thank you. Bea packed it; you brought it. Excellent division of labor.” The delivery is complete, with one useful distinction explored: queries and keys determine the attention weights, while values supply the weighted mixture.

sources.title: Your pasted material · excerpt 1
sources.text:
Editorial learning notes about the original Transformer architecture, based on Vaswani et al., Attention Is All You Need, sections 3.1–3.5: https://arxiv.org/html/1706.03762v7

Token identity and sequence order
The model represents tokens using learned embedding vectors. In the original architecture, positional encodings are added to those embeddings to provide information about sequence order. The same token can have the same initial embedding at two locations while the added positional information differs. Numerical changes do not by themselves prove understanding. These notes describe an illustrative small model; real embedding coordinates do not have assigned human-readable meanings.

Scaled dot-product attention
Queries and keys determine comparison scores. Divide their dot products by the square root of the key dimension, then apply softmax to get weights. Multiply those weights by the value vectors and sum the contributions. The result is a weighted mixture of values rather than simply selecting the strongest key. Holding queries and keys fixed while changing values leaves the attention weights fixed but can change the output mixture. Q, K and V in a model come from learned projections of representations; a small demonstration can provide explicit illustrative vectors without claiming that they were trained on language.

Causal masking in decoder self-attention
The original decoder's self-attention restricts each input position to itself and earlier input positions. The prediction target is shifted: that current input helps predict the next token. Future input positions are masked before softmax, receiving zero attention weight. Changing later inputs must not change an earlier position's output under this causal mask. Blocking everything is not a valid repair because a row still needs permitted context. Encoder self-attention does not use this same causal restriction. This is a demonstration of selected computations, not a whole trained language model; full Transformer blocks also include other components such as feed-forward layers, residual connections and normalization.

objectives.title: Distinguish attention weights from the weighted output
objectives.claim: Queries and keys determine attention weights through scaled dot products and softmax; those weights combine value vectors into an output. Holding queries and keys fixed while changing values preserves the weights but can change the output.
objectives.boundaries: Focus on one scaled dot-product attention computation, not a full Transformer or trained language model. All numerical vectors are illustrative, not learned language embeddings; coordinates have no assigned human-readable meanings. Exclude positional encoding and causal masking.
objectives.misconception: Attention simply returns the value associated with the strongest key, so unchanged weights imply an unchanged output.

puzzles.title: Distinguish attention weights from the weighted output
puzzles.instructions: Help bird courier Moss open the harbor bridge, then meet Bea to raise the parcel platform. Collect the parcel and return it to Moss. Explore how attention weights differ from the output they produce. Every numerical vector here is illustrative—not a learned language embedding.

config.briefing: Help bird courier Moss open the harbor bridge, then meet Bea to raise the parcel platform. Collect the parcel and return it to Moss. Explore how attention weights differ from the output they produce. Every numerical vector here is illustrative—not a learned language embedding.
config.modelNotes: Objective: attention-roles. Approach: simulation. Source: text-1. This models one query attending to two keys, with scalar values. Scores are q·k/√d, weights are softmax(scores), and output = wA·vA + wB·vB using fractional weights. Here d = 1; all vector coordinates and outputs are dimensionless, and weights are displayed as percentages. The sample docks supply illustrative value pairs; the dial supplies an illustrative query. Keys are fixed within each case. Changing values alone cannot change the weights. Coordinates have no assigned human-readable meanings. The harbor mechanisms are fictional rewards, not parts of a Transformer. Learned projections, positional encoding, masking, and full Transformer blocks are outside this demonstration.

controls.label: Value-pair dock — carry one sample token to a dock

tasks.title: Moss: change the mixture, preserve the weights
tasks.prompt: Illustrative setup: kA = +1, kB = −1, d = 1. Open the bridge with A's weight between 85% and 90% and the weighted output between 6.8 and 7.3. Read the starting weights and output. Carry the single sample token to another value-pair dock, then compare readings before activating. The query dial is available, but changing values alone preserves weights. Hint: multiply each value by its fractional weight, then add; the strongest key does not simply return its value.
tasks.successFeedback: Bridge open! A still receives about 88.1% of the attention, but changing the values raises the output to about 7.05. It is not 8: B's nonzero weight also contributes. Queries and keys set the weights; values supply what gets mixed.
tasks.failureFeedback: Check both target ranges. If A's weight is outside its range, explore the query dial. If the weight is suitable but the output is not, compare the value pairs while leaving the query unchanged. Use percentages divided by 100 in the weighted sum.

tasks.title: Bea: apply the distinction after the keys change
tasks.prompt: Across the bridge, Bea's illustrative setup has kA = −1, kB = +1, d = 1. Raise the parcel platform with B's weight between 85% and 90% and the weighted output between 5.3 and 5.7. Compare the new starting readings with Moss's case. Predict which value pair can meet the output range without disturbing suitable weights, move the single token, and check your prediction. Activate when both targets are met, then collect the parcel and return to Moss.
tasks.successFeedback: Platform raised! Reversing the keys made B receive about 88.1% of the attention at the same query. The successful mixture is about 5.52, not the strongest key's value of 6. Changing values preserved this case's weights while changing its output.
tasks.failureFeedback: The keys have changed, so check which weight is larger rather than reusing the bridge's conclusion. Once B's weight is in range, estimate each dock's weighted mixture. Both values contribute; matching only the strongest key's value is not enough.

discoveries.title: Weights Are Not the Output
discoveries.text: In scaled dot-product attention, queries and keys produce scores q·k/√d; softmax turns those scores into weights. Those weights multiply the values, and the contributions are summed. Here, d = 1 and output = wA·vA + wB·vB, using fractional weights. Holding queries and keys fixed preserves the weights when values change, but the output can change. This is a weighted mixture, not simply the value belonging to the strongest key. Source: text-1. All numbers are illustrative—not learned language embeddings.

discoveries.title: Changed Keys, Same Rule
discoveries.text: This case reverses the illustrative keys: kA = −1 and kB = +1. At q = +1, B now receives about 88.1% of the attention. Changing values alone still preserves those weights while potentially changing the output. In a model, Q, K and V come from learned projections of representations; this small experiment uses explicit illustrative vectors instead. Their coordinates have no assigned human-readable meanings. It demonstrates one attention computation, not a full Transformer or trained language model. Source: text-1.
